headline: Where did the fluke go? Ocean structure, and why your back-bay drops are coming up empty
subhead: Doormats are pushing offshore ahead of the fall run, but the inlets are paying off in albies, bonito, and blues for anyone willing to switch gears.
body_markdown:
Why are the fluke drops that produced all summer suddenly quiet? That's the question coming across the counter this week, and it's a fair one, because the sod banks behind Absecon and the deeper holes off Great Egg were holding fish through mid-August. The answer is the calendar. Early September is when doormat-class fluke abandon the back bay for ocean-side structure — reef sites, wrecks, and the deeper bars off Ocean City and Townsends Inlet — and that shift is happening on schedule this year. You'll still find keeper fluke, but the numbers game that defined July and August is over in the bay. If you want fluke this week, fish the structure, not the flats.

What's replacing that program is a genuinely strong inshore migration bite. Surf temps have held in the 73 to 75-degree range along the beachfront, and that warmth has kept false albacore and bonito working peanut bunker pods from Brigantine down through Sea Isle and into Townsends Inlet. We flagged this exact pattern last week — said the warm filament pushing albies and bonito into Rhode Island waters would widen the window down the Jersey coast — and that's exactly what's playing out. The bite isn't guesswork anymore; it's showing up at the inlets on the right tide stage, consistently enough that the tackle counter is selling out of small metal by Thursday.

Striped bass are a different story, and it's worth being straight about it. Bunker schools are building in the back bays and along the beachfront, but with water still sitting in the low-to-mid 70s, the bass are staged on that bait rather than committing to real blitz behavior. That matches what the moon is telling us — we're building toward full around September 6-7, and a fuller moon means stronger tidal push, which is usually the mechanism that tightens scattered bait into a target bass can actually work efficiently. Until that happens, striper fishing in this zone is a stealth game: small numbers, mostly at first light, mostly on bait imitations worked slow along current seams rather than anything resembling a top-water blitz.

The albie and bonito bite is best worked on the outgoing tide at Absecon Inlet, particularly the last two hours of the ebb when peanut bunker get pushed out of the back channels and stack against the jetty rocks. Half-ounce epoxy jigs in bunker or silverside patterns, and small Deadly Dicks, are the go-to — fast retrieve, no hesitation, because these fish are chasing, not inspecting. Great Egg Inlet is fishing the same way off the Longport side, with the deeper cut holding fish on the last of the ebb into the first hour of the new flood. Townsends Inlet has been more of a bonito show than albie, with fish showing tight to the jetty rocks on calm mornings — small profile metal, 1/2 to 3/4 ounce, cast right up against the rocks and worked back with a steady jigging motion.

Bluefish remain the most dependable bite in the zone right now, and that's holding true to what warm water has been doing basin-wide all summer. Cocktail blues in the 2 to 4-pound range are mixing right in with the albie and bonito schools at all four inlets — Absecon, Great Egg, Townsends, and the surf off Stone Harbor — chewing through peanut bunker pods with the same aggression that's been consistent since July. If metal isn't producing on a given tide, a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig soaking in the wash off Ocean City or Stone Harbor beach will pick up blues reliably, especially in the two hours around high tide when bait gets pushed tight to the beach.

Weakfish have been a minor but real presence in the deeper holes of the back bay — Absecon Channel and the Great Egg back bay both giving up a few fish in the 16 to 20-inch class on Gulp swimming mullets fished on light jigheads, drifted slow along the channel edges on the last of the outgoing. Kingfish are still working the surf troughs at Ocean City and Sea Isle on bloodworm and Fishbites, a steady but modest bite typical for this point in the season. Triggerfish, when they show, are turning up around the inlet jetty structure and pilings at Absecon and Townsends — bits of clam or crab fished tight to the rocks will find them, though this remains an incidental catch rather than a target species most days.

Looking ahead, the next 48 to 72 hours should mirror what's already working: strong albie and bonito action at the inlets on the outgoing tide, steady bluefish, and striped bass that stay staged on bait rather than committed until that building moon tightens the bunker schools further. If a real cool front pushes through in the next week to ten days — and there's reason to think one is coming as we move deeper into September — that's the trigger that should finally break the first legitimate fall blitz open somewhere along this beachfront. Until then, the smart plan is simple: fish the inlets on the ebb for albies and bonito, work ocean structure for fluke, and treat any bass you find as a bonus rather than the main event.
